blocks.name: Drawing and interpreting labour market diagrams

blocks.text: Drawing and interpreting labour market diagrams

blocks.md:
- The **labour marke**t is a type of ***factor market***
- **Factor markets** follow exactly the same rules as** product markets**

  - They are affected by changes to price, demand and supply
  - They are affected by the **price elasticity of demand and supply**
- **Labour market equilibrium** occurs where the **demand for labour (D**<sub>**L**</sub>**)** is equal to the **supply of labour (S**<sub>**L**</sub>**)**

  - The D<sub>L</sub> is the demand **by firms** for workers
  
    - Firms **demand more** labour as the wage rate decreases, which results in a downward-sloping demand curve
  - The S<sub>L</sub> is the supply of labour **by workers**
  
    - Workers **supply more** labour as the wage rate increases, which results in an upward-sloping supply curve
- Individual firms are ***price takers*** in the labour market, as they have to accept the **wage rate **that workers are being paid in the industry

  - If they offer a** lower wage,** they will likely struggle to recruit workers
  - If they offer a **higher wage,** there will be a large number of workers applying to work there

blocks.alt: A supply and demand graph for graphic designers' wages, with the wage rate on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal; equilibrium at point (W, Q).
blocks.caption: In the labour market for graphic designers, the equilibrium wage rate is W and the equilibrium quantity is Q. At this point the DL = SL

blocks.md:
- The market for graphic designers is in **equilibrium where D**<sub>**L**</sub>** = S**<sub>**L **</sub>
- The **equilibrium wage** is W and the **quantity** of labour is Q
- There is ***no excess supply*** of labour
- There is ***no excess demand*** for labour

blocks.name: Changes in demand and supply in the labour market
blocks.definition: Changes in demand and supply in the labour market

blocks.text: Changes in demand and supply in the labour market

blocks.alt: Labour market graph showing shifts in demand, with supply curve intersecting demand curves at equilibrium prices, highlighting a demand increase.
blocks.caption: An increase in the demand for labour increases the equilibrium wage rate

blocks.md:
- **Cause**

  - Economic growth, increased demand for goods and services, higher labour productivity
- **Effect on diagram**

  - Labour demand curve shifts **right** (*D1 → D2*)
- **Result**

  - Higher equilibrium wage rate (*W1 → W2*) and more labour employed (*Q1 → Q2*)

blocks.alt: Graph showing supply and demand for labour with wage per hour on y-axis and quantity on x-axis. Includes supply shift and equilibrium prices marked.
blocks.caption: An increase in the supply of labour decreases the equilibrium wage rate

blocks.md:
- **Cause**

  - *Immigration*, higher working‑age population, more flexible working patterns
- **Effect on diagram**

  - Labour supply curve shifts **right** (*S1 → S2*)
- **Result**

  - Lower equilibrium wage rate (*W1 → W2*) and more labour employed (*Q1 → Q2*)

blocks.alt: Graph depicting shifts in labour market; shows supply and demand curves, two equilibrium prices, and a blue arrow indicating demand shift.
blocks.caption: A decrease in the demand for labour decreases the equilibrium wage rate

blocks.md:
- **Cause**

  - Recession, automation replacing workers, falling demand for goods
- **Effect on diagram**

  - Labour demand curve shifts **left** (*D1 → D2*)
- **Result**

  - Lower equilibrium wage rate (*W1 → W2*) and less labour employed (*Q1 → Q2*)

blocks.alt: Labour market graph showing wage and quantity, with supply and demand curves. Equilibrium prices at $30 and $40, supply shift indicated by an arrow.
blocks.caption: A decrease in the supply of labour increases the equilibrium wage rate

blocks.md:
- **Cause**

  - Ageing population, *emigration*, higher welfare benefits reducing incentives to work
- **Effect on diagram**

  - Labour supply curve shifts **left** (*S1 → S2*)
- **Result**

  - Higher equilibrium wage rate (*W1 → W2*) and less labour employed (*Q1 → Q2*)

blocks.name: Analysing the PED and PES of labour
blocks.definition: Analysing the PED and PES of labour

blocks.text: Analysing the PED and PES of labour

blocks.md:
- Consider the** labour market** for NBA basketball players
- In 2022, ***LeBron James*** received a salary of \$45m

blocks.alt: Supply and demand graph for labour, with wages on the Y-axis and quantity on the X-axis, intersected by a basketball and a trainer.
blocks.caption: The impact of inelastic demand and supply in the labour market

blocks.md:
- **D**<sub>**L**</sub>** **is the demand for labour **from the basketball clubs**
- **S**<sub>**L**</sub> is the supply of labour **by the basketball players**
- The **demand **for highly skilled players is very **price inelastic**

  - Clubs want the very best players, almost irrespective of what they **cost**
- The **supply** of highly skilled players is also very **price inelastic**

  - A significant increase in price will have little impact on the quantity of labour supplied in the market, as it takes years to develop ***LeBron James-type*** skills
- The **market equilibrium** is found at W<sub>1</sub>Q<sub>1 </sub>- a **high price** and relatively **low quantity**
- Consider the** labour market** for labourers on a building site

- **D**<sub>**L**</sub>** **is the demand for labour **from the building company for labourers**
- **S**<sub>**L**</sub> is the supply of labour **by people willing to work on a building site**
- The **demand **for workers is very **price elastic**

  - If wages dropped a little, then firms would respond quickly by **employing more workers**
- The **supply** of workers is also very **price elastic**

  - Due to it being an unskilled job, there would quickly be an increase in the **supply of labour** if wages were to increase
- The **market equilibrium** is found at W<sub>1</sub>Q<sub>1 </sub>- a **low price** and relatively **high quantity**
